question: Spanish media recently reported cases of Spanish labour migrants being exploited in the Netherlands. Workers are promised decent conditions but instead face exploitation in economically depressed sectors. Temporary agencies recruit workers and control every aspect of their lives, including housing, while denying them permanent contracts.

The resulting subcontracting chains create deliberate confusion about who is accountable for these workers. They often earn only the minimum wage, with housing costs deducted directly from their pay. 1.

The Netherlands has still not transposed the minimum wage directive1 in national law. What actions is the Commission planning to take to ensure that the Netherlands will transpose this directive as soon as possible?

Temporary agents deduct the costs of housing from the minimum wage these workers earn. How does the Commission interpret this in the light of the minimum wage directive, which explicitly limits the possibilities for exceptions to the minimum wage?

What action will the Commission take to ensure that subcontracting chains are reduced in the EU, in order to ensure that those who are responsible for the workers will be held responsible? Will the Commission present a legislative proposal to limit the chain of subcontracting?
OJ L 275, 25.10.2022, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2022/2041/oj.
answer: EN On behalf of the European Commission (26.1.2026) The deadline for transposing Directive (EU) 2022/20411 elapsed on 15 November 2024, and the Netherlands has not yet notified its transposition. My services have contacted the Dutch authorities in this regard and are closely monitoring the state of play.

If and to the extent needed, the Commission can start an infringement procedure against any Member State that has not yet transposed this Directive. Directive 2008/104/EC2 establishes the principle of equal treatment for agency workers in user companies from the first day of their assignment. Equal treatment applies to basic working and employment conditions, notably pay and working time.

As concerns the deduction of the cost of housing from the minimum wage, Article 6 of Directive (EU) 2022/2041 requires Member States to ensure that such deductions respect the principles of non-discrimination and proportionality, the latter including the pursuit of a legitimate aim3. The Commission will carefully examine this deduction in the context of its assessment of the transposition of this Directive.

On 4 December 2025, the Commission launched the first phase consultation of social partners on a potential Quality Jobs Act, to gather their views on the need for and possible direction of EU action4. This consultation covers inter alia issues relating to subcontracting.

Prevention of labour exploitation of mobile and migrant workers is also being considered in the context of the future Fair Labour Mobility Package5. The Package will address the challenges emerging from the increasing posting of third country nationals and from crossborder provision of services by temporary work agencies and recruitment intermediaries, including in long and complex sub-contracting chains.
